content.text: The verifier confirms the classification but flags the deterministic check failure as a definitional artefact. I'll repair the finding by anchoring the "Either Party" language to the defined-term chain that establishes Customer as a holder of the right.

input.quote: Either Party may terminate this Agreement for any reason following the Initial Term upon ninety (90) days written notice to the other Party.
input.rationale:
COMPLIANT AT FALLBACK. No redline required.

Resolving the deterministic check: the "Customer convenience termination present" check failed only because ¶4(a) confers the right on "Either Party" rather than naming Customer expressly. The defined-term chain closes that gap. Paragraph p0000 provides that The Associated Press is "the 'Customer'" and that "Each of Customer and Kubient may be referred to herein individually as a 'Party'." Customer is therefore a Party, and the ¶4(a) grant that "Either Party may terminate this Agreement for any reason following the Initial Term upon ninety (90) days written notice to the other Party" vests a convenience right in us directly. The right is present; only its phrasing is generic.

Material terms against the rule:
1. Customer convenience right — present, no-cause ("for any reason"), on 90 days' written notice. That is within the fallback's 60–90 day band.
2. Lock-out period — the Initial Term is exactly one (1) year with 1-year auto-renewals. The no-convenience window is not a term "longer than 12 months," so the walk-away test (no Customer convenience right in a multi-year term) is not triggered.
3. Early-termination cost — no fee or penalty. Kubient's entitlement to "all fees generated during the termination period" is revenue share actually earned across the 90-day notice window, at or under the fallback's 3-months'-fees cap, and is consideration for services rendered rather than an exit charge.
4. Vendor convenience right — 90 days' notice, which meets rather than breaches the walk-away floor of "fewer than 90 days."

Noted, not redlined (minor sub-elements): (a) 90 days' notice rather than the preferred 30; (b) Vendor may exit at any time after the Initial Term rather than strictly at the end of a renewal term. Item (b) is the closest call against the fallback's "only at the end of a term" wording, but the right is fully reciprocal on identical 90-day notice within a short 1-year renewal cycle, so it benefits us equally and does not fail the fallback on a material term. (c) No pro-rata prepaid-fee refund, which is moot because §5 (p0023) is a pure revenue share under which Kubient collects from Advertisers and remits to Customer within seven days under sequential liability — Customer prepays nothing and so has nothing to reclaim.

Forward-looking note for the deal team (outside this rule's scope): if the commercial model shifts from revenue share to any prepaid or subscription fee basis, the absent refund mechanic becomes live and T4C should be re-run against the revised fee clause.
